questions.question: Why register a tool's schema separately from its handler?
options: Because JSON Schema keywords are only valid when the schema file is written in YAML rather than JSON
So the validator stays a pure function over data, and the handler stays opaque, arbitrary code
Because a Python handler function cannot serialize its return value into a JSON response
Because every schema must be compiled into a callable validator function before the registry starts
questions.explanation: Keeping the schema as data and the handler as code lets the validator be a pure function over the schema tree. Serialization, file format, and compilation are unrelated to the separation.

questions.question: Which keywords are intentionally outside the subset this lesson implements?
options: type, properties, and required, which describe the shape of an object's own fields and which are mandatory
minLength, maxLength, and pattern, which constrain the length and format of individual string values
oneOf, anyOf, allOf, and $ref, which add cycles and reference resolution the validator avoids
items and enum, which constrain the elements of an array and restrict a value to a fixed, closed set
questions.explanation: The omitted keywords add cycles and reference resolution. We keep the subset linear so the validator stays a single recursive walk; the other three groups are all part of the implemented subset.

questions.question: Why does register() reject duplicates by default?
options: Because the underlying dict the registry uses can only hold one key per tool name at a time
Silent overwrites of a tool name are the usual cause of production tool-catalog drift
Because a schema that already validated once cannot be re-validated against a new handler
Because a handler function, once registered, is immutable and cannot be reassigned later
questions.explanation: Forcing override=True surfaces the case where two parts of the code intend to own the same tool name. It has nothing to do with dict limits, re-validation, or immutability.

questions.question: What does the validator do when a schema specifies type integer but receives the value True?
options: The validator treats the boolean True as equivalent to the integer 1 and lets it pass the check silently
The validator raises an unhandled exception rather than returning a structured, catchable type error
The validator silently coerces the boolean into an integer value before continuing with validation
The validator returns a type error, since it filters bool out of the integer check despite bool being a subclass of int
questions.explanation: Python bool is a subclass of int, but the validator filters bool out of the integer check. JSON booleans and integers are distinct, so it neither passes silently, coerces, nor crashes.

questions.question: When the input object is {'user': {'email': 0}} and the schema requires user.email to be a string, what is the error path?
options: /user/email, since the JSON pointer encodes the descent through user then email
/, because the pointer always starts at the schema root regardless of nesting depth
/user, because the pointer stops one level short of the field that actually failed
user.email, since dotted paths are how the validator reports nested field errors
questions.explanation: JSON pointer encodes the descent through user then email as /user/email — it does not stop early, stay at root, or use dotted notation.

questions.question: Why is the registry not a security boundary?
options: Because handler functions registered in this system are always declared async and run outside the caller
Because the schema is expressed as JSON text rather than as a compiled binary validation format
Because a handler can still misbehave once its arguments pass validation, since shape is not behavior
Because the registry and every handler it tracks execute in the same process as the caller
questions.explanation: The registry checks shape. Behavior, timeouts, and isolation belong to the dispatcher and the sandbox — async-ness, JSON format, and in-process execution are not the reason.
